newsitem.title: UK: Union ban lifted at British eavesdropping centre.
newsitem.headline: Union ban lifted at British eavesdropping centre.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Thursday delighted trade unionists by lifting a ban on union activity at the GCHQ electronic eavesdropping centre which has for decades formed a key part of the West's intelligence network.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said the government had decided to "right a long-standing wrong" by allowing the 4,900 staff at the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) to join the union of their choice.
But he said they would still not be allowed to strike or take other action which would disrupt work at the highly sensitive establishment in Cheltenham, western England.

Union membership has been banned since 1984 when then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher declared that for workers at GCHQ it represented a conflict of interest. She accused union officials of exploiting the sensitivity of the security centre to further their pay claims.

Thatcher's Conservative government offered each unionist 1,000 pounds ($1,640) in compensation. Fourteen union loyalists who refused to give up their membership were sacked, making the issue a cause celebre among left-wingers who believed Thatcher had acted under pressure from the U.S. government.

Cook, whose party pledged to restore union rights in its manifesto for Britain's May 1 election, said that in return for doing so, the government intended to negotiate a "collective agreement on no disruption of work" with the unions.

"GCHQ staff make a valuable contribution to protecting the liberties and freedom of our country," he said in a statement. "Today's move enables them to share fully in one of the most important liberties that they defend."

GCHQ intercepts communications, using spy satellites and electronic listening and decoding devices, to gather information about terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, drug trafficking and the availability of commodities such as oil.

John Monks, general secretary of Britain's Trades Union Congress, said the GCHQ union ban had been a blot on Britain's reputation for democracy and human rights and had often been criticised by the International Labour Organisation.
"The previous government's belief that free trade unionism compromised national security was always an unjustified slur against the trade union movement," he said.
"The end of the ban will therefore be widely welcomed...Today is a day for celebration," Monks added.
Cook said those former employees who were sacked for continuing their union membership will now be free to apply for re-employment if they are still of working age.
"Each case will be treated sympathetically, within the normal Civil Service rules for such employment," he said.
